```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment  = "#>"
)
library(inshape)
library(tibble)
```

Register microdata comes in a few shapes: one row per unit, one row per
unit and period (a panel), or one row per spell with a start and an end.
Every analysis assumes the shape is right, and the errors that break it are
silent: a duplicated key multiplies rows in a join, a missing year looks
like an exit, an overlapping spell gives a person two addresses at once.

inshape checks the shape before anything is built on it, in two steps.
The `describe_*()` functions look at the structure and judge nothing; the
`ensure_*()` functions are *checkpoints*: each states one rule, warns or
aborts with the rows that break it, and returns the data, so it sits in a
pipeline. Most rules are about structure; `ensure_none()`, `ensure_all()`
and `ensure_empty()` take any rule dplyr can express.

| Function | The rule | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| `describe_key()` | (look) duplicated keys, exact copies vs. conflicts | a summary |
| `describe_panel()` | (look) units, gaps, entries, exits, patterns | a summary |
| `describe_spells()` | (look) gaps, transfers, overlapping and nested spells | a summary |
| `describe_varying()` | (look) which columns vary within units | a summary |
| `describe_codes()` | (look) how the codes of a column change over periods | a summary |
| `describe_changes()` | (look) what changed between two extracts | a summary |
| `describe_match()` | (look) what a join of two tables will do | a summary |
| `ensure_codes()` | a coded column holds only codes from the code list | the data |
| `ensure_complete()` | the columns named have no missing values | the data |
| `ensure_constant()` | sex, birth date and the like are constant within a unit | the data |
| `ensure_unique()` | the key columns identify each row | the data |
| `ensure_balanced()` | every unit is observed in every period, or has no gaps | the data |
| `ensure_no_overlap()` | a unit's spells do not overlap | the data |
| `ensure_no_gaps()` | a unit's spells leave no gaps between them | the data |
| `ensure_within()` | no rows after death or emigration, or before birth | the data |
| `ensure_valid_spells()` | a spell has a start and does not end before it | the data |
| `ensure_matched()` | every key occurs in a reference register | the data |
| `ensure_panel()` | the key is complete and unique, and no unit skips a period | the data |
| `ensure_spells()` | the unit is complete, the spells valid and not overlapping | the data |
| `ensure_lookup()` | a lookup table's key is unique and covers the data | the data |
| `ensure_none()` | no row matches a condition (`NA` passes) | the data |
| `ensure_all()` | every row meets a condition (`NA` fails) | the data |
| `ensure_empty()` | a violation set you built yourself has no rows | the set |
| `tally_violations()` | (count) violations for many rules at once | a tally |
| `describe_transitions()` | (look) how a status changes from one observation to the next | a summary |
| `ensure_transitions()` | a status does not change in a forbidden way | the data |
| `merge_spells()` | (fix) spells recorded as several, merged | merged spells |
| `fill_panel()` | (fix) missing unit-periods added as rows | the filled panel |
| `carry_status()` | (fix) a status that holds once reached, carried forward | the data plus status |
| `spells_to_panel()` | (conversion) spells to a period panel | a panel |
| `add_spell_status()` | (conversion) status from spells on an existing panel | the data plus status |

## Look first: `describe_panel()` and `describe_key()`

A rule is easier to choose when you have seen the data. `describe_panel()`
summarises a panel in one pass: how many units are observed throughout,
who enters and leaves when, where the gaps are, and which participation
patterns are common, as Stata's `xtdescribe` does.

```{r}
persons <- tibble(
  cpr  = c("a", "a", "a", "b", "b", "c", "d", "d", "d", "d"),
  year = c(2020, 2021, 2022, 2020, 2022, 2022, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2022)
)

describe_panel(persons, cpr, year)
```

A period with no units, or a sudden fall in `units`, is the sign of a
broken extract. The counts are there to use as well, e.g.
`describe_panel(persons, cpr, year)$by_period`.

`describe_key()` looks at a key. When it is not unique, the question is
what the duplicates are: exact copies, which can be dropped, or rows that
disagree, which need a rule. It tells them apart and names the columns the
copies disagree in:

```{r}
firms <- tibble(
  cvr      = c("1", "1", "2", "2", "3"),
  year     = 2024,
  industry = c("A", "A", "B", "C", "A")
)

describe_key(firms, cvr, year)
```

## Keys: `ensure_unique()`

Duplicate keys are the most common error in register data, and the most
costly one sits right before a join. A lookup table with a duplicated key
makes `left_join()` multiply rows without a word. Check the key first:

```{r}
df <- tibble(
  cvr  = c("11111111", "22222222", "11111111"),
  year = c(2024, 2024, 2024)
)

df |>
  ensure_unique(cvr, year, warn_msg = "Duplicate company-years")
```

The reported rows carry a `dupid`, so the copies in each group sit
together.

Every failure is laid out the same way: what broke, how many rows, counts
that show the pattern, the first rows, and the next step as code to copy.
Here some duplicates are exact copies and one person has two
municipalities in the same year:

```{r}
persons_2019 <- tibble(
  cpr  = c("a", "a", "b", "b", "c", "c", "d"),
  year = c(2019, 2019, 2019, 2019, 2021, 2021, 2021),
  kom  = c("955", "955", "955", "956", "957", "957", "955")
)

ensure_unique(persons_2019, cpr, year)
```

The hints never choose for you. Exact copies can only be dropped one way,
so the hint is the code; copies that differ need a rule for which to keep,
so the code has a hole, `<column>`, for you to fill.

## Missing values: `ensure_complete()`

Some columns an analysis cannot do without: the id, the date, the outcome.
A missing value in them drops the row from a model without a word, or
becomes a group of its own in a count. `ensure_complete()` requires the
columns named to have a value in every row, or all columns if none are
named. The reported rows carry a `missing` column that names the columns
missing in each:

```{r}
register <- tibble(
  cpr  = c("a", "b", NA, "d"),
  born = as.Date(c("1980-05-01", NA, NA, "1975-02-11")),
  sex  = c("F", "M", "F", NA)
)

ensure_complete(register, cpr, born)
```

Missing means `NA`; an empty string is a value.

## Panels: `ensure_balanced()`

A yearly register extract is a panel: one row per person (or company) and
year. Whether it is *balanced*, every unit present in every year, decides
which methods are valid and often reveals a broken extract.

```{r}
panel <- tibble(
  cpr  = c("a", "a", "a", "b", "b", "c"),
  year = c(2020, 2021, 2022, 2020, 2022, 2022)
)

ensure_balanced(panel, cpr, year)
```

Real populations are rarely balanced. People are born, die and migrate.
What usually *should* hold is that a unit, once present, does not skip a
year before it leaves. `gaps_only = TRUE` checks that: `c` entering in
2022 is fine, `b` missing in 2021 is not.

```{r}
ensure_balanced(panel, cpr, year, gaps_only = TRUE)
```

By default the expected years are those found in the data, so a year that
was never loaded goes unnoticed. State the years you expect to catch that
as well:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
ensure_balanced(panel, cpr, year, periods = 2015:2024, gaps_only = TRUE)
```

When the gaps are real, `fill_panel()` adds them as rows with the unit and
the period filled in and everything else missing, so a count per year sees
them. It says how many rows it added:

```{r}
filled <- fill_panel(panel, cpr, year)
```

## Status over time: `describe_transitions()`, `ensure_transitions()` and `carry_status()`

A status that follows a person, such as education, can only change in
some ways. `describe_transitions()` counts the units going from each
status to each other between two observations, so the impossible ones show
as cells that should be empty:

```{r}
education <- tibble(
  cpr    = c("a", "a", "a", "b", "b", "c", "c"),
  year   = c(2019, 2020, 2021, 2019, 2020, 2019, 2021),
  status = c("not started", "enrolled", "completed",
             "enrolled", "completed", "completed", "not started")
)

describe_transitions(education, cpr, year, status)
```

`ensure_transitions()` forbids them, as pairs or as a final status nothing
may follow:

```{r}
ensure_transitions(education, cpr, year, status, final = "completed")
```

Which of the two observations is wrong, the package cannot know. When you
know that the final status holds, `carry_status()` carries it forward,
into a new column so the original stands beside it, and counts what it
changed:

```{r}
education <- carry_status(education, cpr, year, status, final = "completed")
```

The unit is what `id` says: when a person may complete one education and
start another, use `id = c(cpr, education)`.

## Spells: `ensure_no_overlap()`

The other shape of register data is spells: address periods, employment,
benefit periods. A person has only one address at a time, so overlapping
spells within a person are an error:

```{r}
addresses <- tibble(
  cpr   = c("a", "a", "b", "b"),
  start = as.Date(c("2020-01-01", "2021-01-01", "2020-01-01", "2020-06-01")),
  end   = as.Date(c("2020-12-31", NA,           "2020-06-30", "2021-12-31"))
)

ensure_no_overlap(addresses, cpr, start, end)
```

Spells are closed intervals, and a missing end means the spell is
ongoing. The reported rows carry an `overlap_id` that groups spells
overlapping each other, the same idea as `dupid`.

The opposite rule is `ensure_no_gaps()`: where a person must have an
address every day, a spell that starts later than the day after the
earlier ones ended leaves days without one. The spell after each gap is
reported with the length of the gap, and `max_gap` accepts short ones:

```{r}
moves <- tibble(
  cpr   = c("a", "a", "b", "b"),
  start = as.Date(c("2020-01-01", "2021-01-01", "2020-01-01", "2020-07-04")),
  end   = as.Date(c("2020-12-31", NA,           "2020-06-30", "2021-12-31"))
)

ensure_no_gaps(moves, cpr, start, end)
```

Before requiring that, look at how the spells relate to each other.
`describe_spells()` takes each unit's spells in order and says, for each,
how it relates to the earlier ones: after a gap, adjacent (starting the
day after one ends, often a transfer recorded as two spells), touching on
one shared day, overlapping, nested or a duplicate. In patient registers
up to a quarter of the entries can be such transfers, and counting spells
without merging them first inflates every count.

```{r}
admissions <- tibble(
  cpr   = c("a", "a", "a", "b", "b", "c"),
  start = as.Date(c("2020-01-01", "2020-01-11", "2020-03-01",
                    "2020-01-01", "2020-01-05", "2021-06-01")),
  end   = as.Date(c("2020-01-10", "2020-01-20", "2020-03-05",
                    "2020-01-31", "2020-01-10", NA))
)

describe_spells(admissions, cpr, start, end)
```

`merge_spells()` merges them: by default spells that overlap or follow the
next day become one, from the first start to the latest end, and
`n_spells` counts what was merged. `max_gap = 30` also merges spells less
than a month apart, a readmission counted as the same episode, and `by`
merges only spells that agree in a column such as the employer:

```{r}
merge_spells(admissions, cpr, start, end)
```

## Attributes of the unit: `describe_varying()` and `ensure_constant()`

Sex and birth date belong to the person, not to the year, yet a panel
repeats them on every row, and a person with two values is an error,
usually of linkage or of a correction applied to some years only.
`describe_varying()` shows which columns vary within units, from the
constant to the varying. A column that varies for a handful of units out
of millions is rarely meant to vary:

```{r}
persons <- tibble(
  cpr    = c("a", "a", "b", "b", "c", "c"),
  year   = c(2020, 2021, 2020, 2021, 2020, 2021),
  sex    = c("F", "F", "M", "F", "M", NA),
  income = c(100, 120, 90, 95, 80, 85)
)

describe_varying(persons, cpr)
```

`ensure_constant()` turns that into a rule and lists every row of the units
that break it. A missing value is not a contradiction, so `c` passes:

```{r}
ensure_constant(persons, cpr, sex)
```

## Codes over time: `describe_codes()` and `ensure_codes()`

Code lists change: municipalities merge, industry codes are revised.
`describe_codes()` shows when each code occurs, so a revision stands out as
a period with many new and many gone codes, and a typo as a code seen once:

```{r}
residents <- tibble(
  year = rep(2018:2021, each = 4),
  municipality = c("955", "956", "957", NA,    "955", "956", "957", "957",
                   "960", "956", "957", "95",  "960", "965", "957", "956")
)

describe_codes(residents, municipality, year)
```

`ensure_codes()` requires the codes of a code list:

```{r}
ensure_codes(residents, municipality, c("955", "956", "957", "960", "965"))
```

## A new extract: `describe_changes()`

A register is delivered again and again, and the same person-year should
not change between deliveries unless it was corrected. `describe_changes()`
compares two extracts by their key:

```{r}
before <- tibble(cpr = c("a", "b", "c"), year = 2023,
                 sex = c("F", "M", "F"), born = c(1950, 1960, NA))
after  <- tibble(cpr = c("a", "b", "d"), year = 2023,
                 sex = c("F", "F", "M"), born = c(1950, 1960, 1990))

describe_changes(before, after, cpr, year)
```

## Within a lifetime: `ensure_within()`

Registers are updated at different times, so a linked extract can hold a
person after death or emigration, or income before birth. `ensure_within()`
requires each row to lie between its own bounds, usually joined on from the
population register. A yearly row counts by the year, so the year of death
itself is fine:

```{r}
panel <- tibble(
  cpr   = c("a", "a", "a", "b", "b"),
  year  = c(2022, 2023, 2024, 2022, 2023),
  born  = as.Date(c("1950-04-01", "1950-04-01", "1950-04-01", "2023-01-10", "2023-01-10")),
  death = as.Date(c("2023-05-01", "2023-05-01", "2023-05-01", NA, NA))
)

ensure_within(panel, year, from = born, to = death)
```

## From spells to a panel: `spells_to_panel()`

`spells_to_panel()` turns spells into one row per unit and year (or
`by = "quarter"`/`"month"`), with the status at primo and ultimo. By
default primo is the previous ultimo, so primo 2021 is the status on 31
December 2020.

In an education register the status is the *outcome* of the spell, passed
or dropped out. With `status_is = "outcome"`, a running spell shows as
`ongoing` and the outcome applies from the end date until a new spell
starts:

```{r}
education <- data.frame(
  cpr    = c("a", "a", "b"),
  start  = as.Date(c("2018-08-15", "2021-08-15", "2019-08-15")),
  end    = as.Date(c("2021-06-20", NA,           "2020-03-01")),
  status = c("passed", "in progress", "dropped out")
)

education |>
  spells_to_panel(cpr, start, end, status,
                  from = 2018, to = 2022,
                  status_is = "outcome", ongoing = "in progress")
```

With the default `status_is = "state"`, the status holds for the whole
spell (enrolled, on leave) and is `NA` outside spells. `from` and `to` give
every unit the same window, which makes a balanced panel.

## Status on a panel you have: `add_spell_status()`

Often the panel exists already, and the spells should only add a status to
it. A `left_join(join_by(between()))` does that until the data gets messy:
overlapping spells duplicate rows, and an ongoing spell with no end matches
nothing. `add_spell_status()` keeps the rows of the panel exactly as they
are and uses the rules of `spells_to_panel()`:

```{r}
population <- data.frame(cpr  = c("a", "a", "b", "c"),
                         year = c(2020, 2021, 2020, 2020))

population |>
  add_spell_status(education, cpr, year, start, end, status,
                   status_is = "outcome", ongoing = "in progress")
```

## Valid boundaries and reference coverage

Validate spell boundaries before checking their relationships. Missing ends
represent ongoing spells; `open_end = FALSE` requires closed spells.

```{r}
ensure_valid_spells(education, start, end)
```

Check that each observation can be linked to a reference register. Duplicate
reference keys do not multiply rows, and missing keys do not match unless
`na_matches = "na"` is specified.

```{r}
observations <- tibble(cpr = c("a", "b", "c"), year = 2020)
reference <- tibble(person_id = c("a", "b"), year = 2020)
ensure_matched(observations, reference, by = c(cpr = "person_id", "year"))
```

## The common checks in one call: `ensure_panel()`, `ensure_spells()` and `ensure_lookup()`

A panel nearly always needs the same three checks: the key is complete,
unique and without gaps. `ensure_panel()` runs them all, also after one has
failed, and shows one overview instead of three messages, each pointing to
the single check that gives the rows:

```{r}
yearly <- tibble(
  cpr  = c("a", "a", "a", "b", "b", "c", "d", "d", "d", "d"),
  year = c(2020, 2021, 2022, 2020, 2022, 2022, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2022)
)

ensure_panel(yearly, cpr, year)
```

`ensure_spells()` does the same for spells: the unit is complete, the spells
are valid and do not overlap, and with `no_gaps = TRUE` leave no gaps.
Overlaps mean nothing until the spells are valid, so they are not checked
until then. `ensure_lookup()` checks a table before a join: its key is
unique, so the join does not multiply rows, and every key of the data is in
it.

```{r}
ensure_lookup(observations, reference, by = c(cpr = "person_id", "year"))
```

The choices are fixed where registers nearly always need the same; a panel
may have late entries and early exits (`gaps_only = TRUE`). For anything
else, run the single checks.

## Before a join: `describe_match()`

`ensure_matched()` asks one question of a join, whether every row finds a
match. `describe_match()` looks at the whole of it first: how many keys are
in both tables, how many only in one, and whether the reference repeats a
key, so that a left join returns more rows than it was given. Here `c` is
not in the register, `d` has no income, and `b` is registered twice:

```{r}
income <- tibble(
  cpr    = c("a", "a", "b", "c", NA),
  year   = c(2023, 2024, 2024, 2024, 2024),
  income = c(10, 12, 7, 9, 3)
)
population_register <- tibble(
  person_id = c("a", "b", "b", "d"),
  kommune   = c("955", "956", "957", "960")
)

describe_match(income, population_register, by = c(cpr = "person_id"))
```

A row with a missing key matches nothing and is counted on its own. The key
must be stated in `by`: a join on whatever names two registers happen to
share is how a wrong key goes unnoticed.

## Codes valid at the observation time

A temporal code list has `code`, `valid_from` and `valid_to`. Bounds are
inclusive, missing bounds are open, and a code may have several intervals.
Time and bounds use the same scale: dates, date-times, or numeric periods.
Missing observation times fail for non-missing codes. `na_ok` controls
missing codes separately.

```{r}
codebook <- tibble(code = c("A", "B"),
                   valid_from = c(2015, 2020), valid_to = c(2019, NA_real_))
coded <- tibble(classification = c("A", "A", "B"), year = c(2019, 2020, 2020))
ensure_codes(coded, classification, codebook, time = year)
```

## Rules of your own: `ensure_none()`, `ensure_all()` and `ensure_empty()`

The structure checks cover the rules every register has. The rest are
particular to a delivery: no negative amounts, every cvr eight digits, a
total that matches its parts. Any rule dplyr can express is a checkpoint,
stated as "the set of violations must be empty".

`ensure_none()` takes the condition for a violating row and returns the
full data, so checks chain before the real work continues:

```{r}
sales <- tibble(
  order_id    = 1001:1006,
  customer_id = c(12, 17, NA, 25, 31, NA),
  amount      = c(250, -40, 120, 80, -15, 300)
)

sales |>
  ensure_none(amount < 0, warn_msg = "Negative amounts") |>
  ensure_none(amount > 1e6) |>
  nrow()
```

Without a message, the condition becomes one, which is often enough at
the console. Give checks that stay in a script a message in your own
words. Messages are shown literally, so `"cvr must match ^\\d{8}$"` is
safe.

The condition follows `filter()`: a row where it is `NA` is not a
violation. `ensure_all()` states the rule positively instead, and there a
row passes only when the condition is `TRUE`, so a missing value is a
violation:

```{r}
sales |>
  ensure_none(customer_id < 0)

sales |>
  ensure_all(customer_id > 0)
```

No customer id is negative, but two are missing. Use `ensure_all()` when a
value has to be present *and* right, and `ensure_none()` when a missing
value is acceptable or a rule of its own, such as `ensure_complete()`.

`ensure_empty()` is the most general form: build the violation set
yourself, with a `filter()` or an anti-join, and pipe it in.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
expected |>
  dplyr::anti_join(delivery, by = "cvr") |>
  ensure_empty(warn_msg = "Firms missing from the delivery")
```

### Many rules at once: `tally_violations()`

A chain of checkpoints stops at the first abort. When a delivery has five
problems, you want to hear about all five in one go. `tally_violations()`
evaluates every rule and counts the violating rows, but never warns or
stops: the checkpoints judge, the tally only counts.

```{r}
report <- sales |>
  tally_violations(
    "Negative amount" = amount < 0,
    "No customer"     = is.na(customer_id),
    "Huge amount"     = amount > 1e6
  )
report
```

`rows` holds the row numbers of each rule's violations. Filtered to the
rules that failed, the tally is itself a violation set. `total` is the
number of rows checked, so the same tally can warn about every broken
rule and stop only for those broken at scale:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
report |>
  dplyr::filter(n > 0) |>
  ensure_empty(warn_msg = "Rules with violations")

report |>
  dplyr::filter(n / total > 0.001) |>
  ensure_empty(abort_msg = "Rules broken by more than 0.1 % of the rows")
```

## Personal data and large registers

inshape is made for interactive review of registers, at the console in
the environment where the data lives. The offending rows of a check are
personal data, so inshape writes nothing to disk, neither rows nor a log.
A failure shows the count and the first rows. Wrap the check in
`violations()` to get all of them, to look at in the session; when the
check passes, it returns no rows:

```{r}
gaps <- violations(ensure_balanced(panel, cpr, year, gaps_only = TRUE))
gaps
```

Whether rows are kept anywhere is for the analysis and its data agreement
to decide. To save them, do it yourself, from the rows `violations()`
returns:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
violations(ensure_none(sales, amount < 0)) |>
  data.table::fwrite("negative_amounts.csv")
```

A DuckDB or Arrow table is checked where it lives, and only the count and
the first rows are fetched into R. See `?checkpoints` for both.
